passages.title: Waiting prepares witnesses for a task larger than their question
passages.summary: The writer opens a second book for Theophilus. The risen Jesus teaches the apostles for forty days. He tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit. They ask if he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He is taken up, and two men in white speak to them. About 120 believers pray together in an upper room. Peter says another witness must take the place of Judas. They pray and cast lots, and the lot falls on Matthias.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches that apostles receive their call through revelation. Why does the replacement need to have accompanied Jesus’ whole ministry?

contextNote.title: Waiting prepares witnesses for a task larger than their question
contextNote.text: The apostles ask about timing in verse 6. Will the kingdom come back to Israel now? Verse 7 says the times are not theirs to know. Verse 8 gives them a task in place of a date. Power will come with the Holy Spirit, not from their own plan. The task moves outward: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. Verse 22 defines a witness: one who saw Jesus from John’s baptism onward.

passages.title: Many languages lead toward shared life
passages.summary: On the day of Pentecost a sound like wind fills the house. Tongues like fire rest on the believers, and they speak in other languages. Jews from many nations hear their own languages. Some are amazed, and others say the speakers are drunk. Peter quotes Joel and says God raised Jesus from the dead. The hearers ask what they should do. Peter tells them to repent and be baptized. About three thousand join, and they share teaching, meals, prayer, and goods.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects the Spirit’s prompting with action. How does baptism lead into shared meals and care for needs?

contextNote.title: Many languages lead toward shared life
contextNote.text: The hearers are cut to the heart and ask what to do (verse 37). Verse 38 answers with repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Verse 39 says how far that gift reaches. It is for the hearers, their children, and all who are far off. Joel’s words in verse 17 already said “all flesh.” The list of nations in verses 9–11 shows who is listening. The limit in verse 39 is God’s call, not place or birth.

passages.title: A healing redirects attention away from the healers
passages.summary: Peter and John go to the temple at the hour of prayer. A man lame from birth asks them for money at the gate. Peter says he has no silver or gold. He tells the man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ. The man leaps, walks, and praises God in the temple. A crowd runs together in Solomon’s porch. Peter says God raised Jesus, whom they had denied. He says they acted in ignorance and calls them to repent.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies bold witness through the Holy Ghost. Why does Peter refuse credit for the man’s changed condition?

contextNote.title: A healing redirects attention away from the healers
contextNote.text: The crowd runs to Peter and John in wonder (verse 11). Verse 12 asks why, and it names their wrong guess. They think the two men’s own power or godliness made him walk. Verse 13 gives the credit to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 16 says faith in Jesus’ name made the man strong. Peter speaks to this crowd about its own acts (verses 13–15). Verse 17 then says they acted in ignorance, and verse 19 offers repentance.

passages.title: A visible witness limits the council's threat
passages.summary: The priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees arrest Peter and John. The next day the rulers ask by what name they acted. Peter says the man stands healed by the name of Jesus. The council sees their boldness and notes they are untrained men. It orders them not to speak in Jesus’ name. Peter and John say they cannot stop telling what they saw. The believers pray for boldness, and the place shakes. They share goods, and Barnabas sells a field for those in need.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches the Spirit’s help in courageous witness. How does the healed man’s presence affect the council’s options?

contextNote.title: A visible witness limits the council's threat
contextNote.text: The council has a problem in verses 14–16. The healed man stands there, and all Jerusalem knows the sign. They cannot deny it, so they try to stop the speech (verse 17). Verse 19 asks them to judge: listen to them or to God. Verse 20 gives the reason the order cannot work. The two men saw and heard these things themselves. Verse 21 shows the result: the council threatens and lets them go.

passages.title: Deceit threatens trust within a sharing community
passages.summary: Ananias and Sapphira sell land and keep part of the price. They bring the rest as if it were the whole. Peter says Ananias lied to God, and Ananias falls dead. Three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and also dies. The apostles heal many in Solomon’s porch. The high priest and the Sadducees jail them, but an angel opens the doors. Before the council Peter says they must obey God rather than men. Gamaliel advises caution, and the apostles are beaten and released.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies continued witness despite opposition. Why does Peter distinguish ownership from the lie about the sale?

contextNote.title: Deceit threatens trust within a sharing community
contextNote.text: Chapter 4 ended with Barnabas giving the full price of a field. Ananias brings a part and lets it stand as the whole (verses 1–2). Verse 4 makes clear what the wrong is. The land was his, and the money was his to use. No rule made him give it all. The wrong is the lie, and verse 4 says it was told to God. Verse 11 reports the result: great fear on the whole assembly.

passages.title: Unequal care produces a shared decision
passages.summary: The number of disciples grows. The Hellenists, Jewish believers who spoke Greek, complain against the Hebrews. Their widows are being missed in the daily serving. The twelve ask the group to choose seven men for this work. The group chooses Stephen, Philip, and five others, and the apostles lay hands on them. The word spreads, and many priests believe. Stephen works signs, and men from a synagogue argue with him. They bring false witnesses and take him before the council.

lds.text: How does the whole group help answer the widows’ complaint?

contextNote.title: Unequal care produces a shared decision
contextNote.text: The complaint in verse 1 is about daily help for widows. The twelve say they should not leave the word to serve tables (verse 2). Verse 3 gives the choice to the whole group. It also sets the test: good report, the Spirit, and wisdom. The apostles keep prayer and the word as their own work (verse 4). Verse 5 says the plan pleased the whole group, and it names the seven. Verse 7 reports the result: the word of God increased.

passages.title: Stephen's answer follows rejected helpers and God's wider presence
passages.summary: The high priest asks Stephen if the charges are true. Stephen answers with Israel’s history. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia and was with Joseph in Egypt. Moses was pushed away by his own people, yet God sent him. The fathers made a calf in the wilderness. They had the tabernacle, and Solomon built a house. Stephen says his hearers resist the Holy Spirit as their fathers did. They stone him, and he prays that the sin not be held against them.

lds.text: The selected lesson warns against resisting the Holy Ghost. How does Stephen’s final prayer answer the violence against him?

contextNote.title: Stephen's answer follows rejected helpers and God's wider presence
contextNote.text: Stephen is charged with speaking against the holy place (6:13–14). His answer shows God at work far from it. God acts in Mesopotamia (verse 2), Egypt (verse 9), and Sinai (verse 30). Verse 33 calls desert ground holy. Verse 48 then says the Most High does not live in houses made by hands. Verses 49–50 quote Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne, and his hand made all things. The charge is about a place, and the answer is about where God is.

passages.title: Scattering brings witness and a question about Scripture
passages.summary: Saul approves of Stephen’s death, and a great persecution scatters the believers. Philip tells the people of Samaria about Christ, and many are baptized. Simon, who had amazed the city with sorcery, is baptized too. Peter and John come and lay hands on them, and they receive the Holy Spirit. Simon offers money for that power, and Peter rebukes him. An angel sends Philip to a desert road. An Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah in his chariot. Philip tells him about Jesus and baptizes him.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects the Spirit’s guidance with helping others understand Jesus. How does the official’s question differ from Simon’s request for power?

contextNote.title: Scattering brings witness and a question about Scripture
contextNote.text: The official has the scroll and reads it aloud (verses 28 and 30). Philip asks if he understands. Verse 31 says he cannot without a guide, and he invites Philip up. His question in verse 34 is exact: does the prophet mean himself or another? Philip starts from that passage and tells him about Jesus (verse 35). Simon wanted to buy a power (verses 18–19). The official asks for an explanation, and then for baptism (verse 36).

passages.title: Saul's changed direction requires other people's trust
passages.summary: Saul travels to Damascus with letters to arrest followers of the Way. A light from the sky stops him, and a voice says it is Jesus. He is blind for three days. The Lord sends a disciple named Ananias to him. Ananias lays hands on Saul, and Saul sees and is baptized. Saul speaks of Jesus in the synagogues, and opponents plot to kill him. Barnabas brings him to the apostles in Jerusalem. Peter heals Aeneas in Lydda and raises Tabitha in Joppa.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches that people can repent and change. Why does Ananias name his fear before approaching Saul?

contextNote.title: Saul's changed direction requires other people's trust
contextNote.text: The Lord tells Ananias to go to Saul (verse 11). Verse 13 is his objection: many have reported Saul’s evil in Jerusalem. Verse 14 adds that Saul holds authority to bind believers in Damascus too. The Lord does not deny the reports. He calls Saul a chosen vessel (verse 15). Ananias goes and calls him “Brother Saul” (verse 17). In verses 26–27 the disciples fear Saul until Barnabas speaks for him.

passages.title: The Spirit's arrival changes Peter's judgment
passages.summary: Cornelius is a centurion in Caesarea who fears God and gives to the poor. An angel tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. Peter sees a sheet full of animals and hears a voice tell him to eat. He refuses, and the voice says not to call unclean what God cleansed. The Spirit tells him to go with the messengers. In Cornelius’s house Peter says God shows no favoritism. The Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers while he speaks. Peter orders that they be baptized.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches God’s acceptance across peoples and gradual revelation. What does the Spirit’s arrival change before Peter orders baptism?

contextNote.title: The Spirit's arrival changes Peter's judgment
contextNote.text: Peter says in verse 28 that a Jew may not visit another nation. God has shown him to call no person unclean. Verse 34 states the lesson: God does not show favoritism. Verses 44–46 then give proof that the Jewish believers can hear. The Gentiles speak in other languages and praise God. Verse 47 asks a question that expects no objection. They have the Spirit “just like us,” so water cannot be refused.

passages.title: Peter must explain the meal and the shared gift
passages.summary: Believers in Jerusalem criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. Peter tells them the vision, the Spirit’s order, and the angel’s message to Cornelius. He says the Spirit fell on that household as on them at the beginning. They fall silent and then glorify God. Scattered believers reach Antioch, and some speak to Greeks. Barnabas comes, and he brings Saul from Tarsus. The disciples are first called Christians in Antioch. They send famine relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies Peter’s explanation as part of gradual revelation. Why does Peter compare the household’s gift with the group’s own beginning?

contextNote.title: Peter must explain the meal and the shared gift
contextNote.text: The charge in verse 3 is about a meal, not about baptism. Peter answers in order (verse 4), and he lists what God did. The vision came three times (verse 10). The Spirit told him to go (verse 12). The Spirit fell as he began to speak (verse 15). Verse 17 ends with a question: who was he to stand against God? Verse 18 shows the hearers accept it: God gave repentance to the Gentiles too.

passages.title: An opened prison meets a closed household gate
passages.summary: King Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword. He arrests Peter during the days of unleavened bread. The assembly prays for Peter. At night an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and the iron gate opens. Peter goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark. A servant named Rhoda hears his voice and runs in without opening the gate. Herod orders the guards put to death. Later he accepts praise as a god, and an angel strikes him.

lds.text: Why does the praying group struggle to believe Rhoda’s report?

contextNote.title: An opened prison meets a closed household gate
contextNote.text: Verse 5 says the assembly prayed constantly for Peter. Verse 12 shows many still praying when he knocks. Yet verse 15 has them call Rhoda crazy. Then they say it must be his angel. They prayed for him and did not expect him at the gate. Peter himself thought the rescue was a vision (verse 9). Verse 16 ends it plainly: they open the gate, see him, and are amazed.

passages.title: A synagogue invitation becomes a dispute over wider hearing
passages.summary: The Holy Spirit tells the assembly at Antioch to set apart Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the sorcerer Elymas opposes them and is struck blind. The proconsul Sergius Paulus believes. In Antioch of Pisidia the synagogue rulers invite Paul to speak. He tells Israel’s history from Egypt to David and says God raised Jesus. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers. Some Jewish hearers contradict Paul, and he turns to the Gentiles. The two are driven out and go on to Iconium.

lds.text: How does the next Sabbath’s crowd change the earlier invitation’s outcome?

contextNote.title: A synagogue invitation becomes a dispute over wider hearing
contextNote.text: The first Sabbath ends well: many Jews and converts follow Paul (verse 43). The turn comes in verses 44–45, when the whole city gathers. Verse 45 says jealousy at the crowds moved those who contradicted him. Verse 46 answers that group in that city. The word had to come to them first, and they pushed it away. Verse 47 quotes Isaiah on a light for the Gentiles. Paul still starts in the synagogue in the next city (14:1).

passages.title: Praise and violence both misunderstand the visiting teachers
passages.summary: In Iconium Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue, and the city divides. They flee a plan to stone them. In Lystra Paul heals a man who had never walked. The crowd calls them Jupiter and Mercury, and a priest brings oxen to sacrifice. The two tear their clothes and say they are only men. Opponents from Antioch and Iconium arrive, and the crowd stones Paul. He gets up and goes on to Derbe. They return through the cities, appoint elders, and report in Antioch.

lds.text: How do the teachers answer praise that gives them divine status?

contextNote.title: Praise and violence both misunderstand the visiting teachers
contextNote.text: The crowd explains the healing in its own terms: gods have come down (verse 11). Verse 15 refuses the honor in two steps. The two are men “of the same nature” as the crowd. Their news is to turn from these things to the living God. Paul quotes no Scripture in this speech. He points to the maker of sky, earth, and sea. Verse 17 names the witness this crowd already has: rain, harvests, and food.

passages.title: A disputed requirement leads to a letter and trusted messengers
passages.summary: Men from Judea teach in Antioch that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute this and go to Jerusalem. The apostles and elders meet. Peter says God gave the Gentiles the Spirit and made no distinction. James quotes the prophets and proposes four things to avoid. They send a letter with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices. Paul and Barnabas then disagree over John Mark and part ways. Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies the meeting’s decision through continuing revelation. Why do trusted messengers accompany the written decision?

contextNote.title: A disputed requirement leads to a letter and trusted messengers
contextNote.text: The question in verses 1 and 5 is whether Gentiles must keep Moses’ law. Peter calls that a yoke their fathers could not bear (verse 10). Verse 28 gives the answer in the letter’s own words. It names two who agree: the Holy Spirit and “us.” The word “burden” answers Peter’s “yoke.” Only four things remain, listed in verse 29. Verse 31 shows how the readers took it: they rejoiced at the encouragement.

passages.title: Lost income becomes a public charge and a prison crisis
passages.summary: Paul takes Timothy with him from Lystra. A vision of a man from Macedonia calls Paul across the sea. In Philippi Lydia, a seller of purple, believes and hosts them. Paul orders a spirit out of a slave girl who told fortunes. Her owners lose their income and accuse Paul and Silas before the magistrates. The two are beaten and jailed, and an earthquake opens the doors at midnight. The jailer and his household are baptized. Paul says they are Romans, and the magistrates come and ask them to leave.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches spiritual guidance and courage when sharing the gospel. How does rescue from suicide lead toward teaching, washed wounds, and a meal?

contextNote.title: Lost income becomes a public charge and a prison crisis
contextNote.text: The jailer was ordered to keep them safely (verse 23). Verse 27 shows what open doors mean to him. He thinks the prisoners are gone, and he draws his sword on himself. Verse 28 stops him with a fact: all are still there. The men he chained now save his life. His question in verse 30 follows: what must he do to be saved? Verses 33–34 show the change: he washes their wounds and feeds them.

passages.title: Paul changes his starting point for different hearers
passages.summary: In Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths. Some believe, and opponents raise a mob against Jason’s house. In Beroea the hearers examine the Scriptures daily. In Athens Paul is troubled by the city’s idols. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus. He speaks of the God who made the world and needs nothing. He quotes their poets and says God will judge through a man he raised. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches that people are God’s children. Why does Paul begin the Athens speech with the hearers’ worship and poetry?

contextNote.title: Paul changes his starting point for different hearers
contextNote.text: In the synagogue Paul argues from the Scriptures (verses 2–3). At the Areopagus he quotes no Scripture. Verse 23 starts with an altar of the Athenians’ own. Its words admit there is a god they do not know. Paul says he will announce that one. He then quotes their poets, not the prophets (verse 28). Verse 31 ends with the same claim: God raised a man from the dead.

passages.title: Teaching develops through work, hospitality, and correction
passages.summary: In Corinth Paul lives and works with Aquila and Priscilla, who are tentmakers. He reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposed, he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid. The proconsul Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish law. Paul sails to Ephesus, Caesarea, and Antioch. In Ephesus Apollos teaches well but knows only John’s baptism.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies courage during Paul’s extended teaching. How does private correction prepare Apollos to help other believers?

contextNote.title: Teaching develops through work, hospitality, and correction
contextNote.text: Verses 24–25 praise Apollos first. He is eloquent, strong in the Scriptures, and accurate about Jesus. One thing is missing: he knows only the baptism of John. Verse 26 shows how the gap is closed. Priscilla and Aquila hear him and take him aside. They explain the way of God “more accurately.” Verses 27–28 show the result: he greatly helps the believers in Achaia.

passages.title: Changed worship threatens a trade and gathers a confused crowd
passages.summary: In Ephesus Paul meets twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism. He baptizes them in Jesus’ name, and they receive the Holy Spirit. He teaches for two years in the school of Tyrannus. Seven sons of Sceva misuse Jesus’ name, and a possessed man beats them. Many burn their books of magic. Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, gathers the craftsmen. A crowd fills the theater and shouts for two hours. The town clerk sends them home and points to the courts.

lds.text: How does Demetrius connect income with religious honor in his appeal?

contextNote.title: Changed worship threatens a trade and gathers a confused crowd
contextNote.text: Verse 25 opens Demetrius’s speech with money. The craftsmen have their wealth from this business. Verse 26 names the threat: Paul says gods made by hands are no gods. Only in verse 27 does he add the honor of Artemis and her temple. The crowd takes up the second reason and shouts her name (verse 28). Verse 32 says most did not know why they had come. The clerk points them to the courts (verses 35–38).

passages.title: Paul's farewell makes care more important than personal gain
passages.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece and returns by way of Troas. There Paul speaks until midnight, and young Eutychus falls from a window. Paul embraces him, and he is brought in alive. At Miletus Paul calls the elders of Ephesus. He says he taught them openly and house to house. He expects chains in Jerusalem and says they will not see him again. He warns of wolves and tells them to guard the flock. They kneel, pray, and weep.

lds.text: Why does Paul connect his own labor with helping weak people?

contextNote.title: Paul's farewell makes care more important than personal gain
contextNote.text: Paul warns in verses 29–30 that some will draw disciples after themselves. Verse 33 sets his own record against that. He wanted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing. Verse 34 says his own hands paid for him and his companions. Verse 35 turns that record into a pattern for the elders. They are to work so that they can help the weak. The saying of Jesus gives the reason: giving is more blessed than receiving.

passages.title: Warnings and an untested accusation lead toward arrest
passages.summary: Paul sails to Tyre and then to Caesarea, where he stays with Philip. The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt. He says Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul says he is ready to die there. James and the elders report a rumor that he teaches Jews to leave Moses. They ask him to join four men in a vow at the temple. Men from Asia see him there and stir up the crowd. Roman soldiers take him, and he asks to speak.

lds.text: Which accusation comes from an assumption rather than witnessed temple entry?

contextNote.title: Warnings and an untested accusation lead toward arrest
contextNote.text: Verse 28 makes two charges: Paul teaches against the temple and brought Greeks in. Verse 29 gives the basis for the second charge. The accusers saw Trophimus with Paul in the city. They “supposed” the rest. Paul was in fact there to complete a purification (verse 26). Verse 34 shows the crowd’s state: the officer could not learn the facts.

passages.title: Paul's defense reaches its breaking point with the Gentile task
passages.summary: Paul speaks to the crowd in Hebrew, and they grow quiet. He says he is a Jew, taught by Gamaliel, and once persecuted the Way. He tells of the light near Damascus and the voice of Jesus. Ananias, a devout man, told him he would be a witness. Later, praying in the temple, he was told to leave Jerusalem. When he says he was sent to the Gentiles, the crowd shouts for his death. The officer orders him flogged. Paul says he is a Roman citizen by birth, and they stop.

lds.text: The selected lesson studies testimony through Paul’s recalled encounter. Which recalled instruction makes the listening crowd demand Paul’s removal?

contextNote.title: Paul's defense reaches its breaking point with the Gentile task
contextNote.text: The crowd listens through the whole account of Jesus’ voice and Ananias. Verse 22 says they listened “until he said that.” The breaking point is verse 21, not the vision. Paul says the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles. He says this came while he prayed in the temple (verse 17). He even objected that Jerusalem knew his past (verses 19–20). The crowd in 21:28 already charged him with bringing Greeks in.

passages.title: A promise of Rome passes through a divided hearing and a hidden plot
passages.summary: Paul tells the council he has lived in good conscience. The high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul says he is a Pharisee, on trial for the hope of resurrection. Pharisees and Sadducees then argue, and the officer pulls him out. That night the Lord tells him he must testify in Rome. More than forty men vow not to eat until they kill him. Paul’s nephew reports the plot to the officer. Soldiers take Paul by night to the governor Felix in Caesarea.

lds.text: How does the nephew’s report change the planned journey?

contextNote.title: A promise of Rome passes through a divided hearing and a hidden plot
contextNote.text: Verse 10 leaves Paul in the barracks after a hearing that settled nothing. The officer feared he would be torn apart. Verse 11 comes that night and gives the one fixed point. As he testified in Jerusalem, he must testify in Rome. A sworn plot tests that word at once (verses 12–13). The way out is ordinary: a nephew hears and reports (verse 16). Verse 23 sends Paul out alive under 470 guards.

passages.title: A delayed hearing preserves the governor's advantage
passages.summary: The high priest Ananias and a speaker named Tertullus bring charges before Felix. Tertullus calls Paul a plague and a leader of the Nazarene sect. He says Paul tried to profane the temple. Paul answers that no one found him arguing or stirring a crowd. He says he worships the God of his fathers and hopes for a resurrection. Felix puts off the case until Lysias comes. He and his wife Drusilla hear Paul, and Felix becomes afraid. He keeps Paul two years and leaves him bound.

lds.text: How do fear and hoped-for money affect Felix’s delay?

contextNote.title: A delayed hearing preserves the governor's advantage
contextNote.text: Felix knows the Way well and still delays the ruling (verse 22). Verse 25 shows one reason. Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and judgment, and Felix is terrified. Verse 26 gives a second reason, and it is money. He hopes Paul will pay for release, so he sends for him often. Verse 27 adds a third: he wants favor with Paul’s accusers. After two years Paul is still bound, with no ruling given.

passages.title: Paul's appeal creates a journey without a clear written charge
passages.summary: Festus replaces Felix, and the chief priests ask him to send Paul to Jerusalem. They plan an ambush on the road. Festus hears the case in Caesarea, and the charges are not proved. He asks if Paul will be tried in Jerusalem. Paul says he stands at Caesar’s court and appeals to Caesar. Festus agrees to send him. King Agrippa and Bernice visit, and Festus explains the case. He brings Paul before them the next day.

lds.text: Why does Festus still need a clear charge after Paul’s appeal?

contextNote.title: Paul's appeal creates a journey without a clear written charge
contextNote.text: Paul’s appeal in verse 11 binds Festus to send him (verse 12). That leaves the governor with a letter he cannot write. Verse 25 says he found nothing deserving death. Verse 26 says he has nothing certain to write to the emperor. Verse 19 shows why: the dispute is about Jesus, whom Paul says is alive. Verse 27 states the difficulty in Festus’s own words. A prisoner sent with no charge makes no sense, so he asks Agrippa’s help.

passages.title: Paul answers a royal hearing by inviting belief
passages.summary: Paul speaks before King Agrippa, Bernice, and Festus. He says he lived as a Pharisee and now stands trial for Israel’s hope. He tells how he jailed the saints and voted for their deaths. He describes the light on the Damascus road and the voice of Jesus. He says he obeyed the vision and taught Jews and Gentiles to repent. Festus shouts that learning has made him mad. Paul asks Agrippa if he believes the prophets. Agrippa says Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects testimony with service to others. Why does Paul exclude his chains from what he wishes for his hearers?

contextNote.title: Paul answers a royal hearing by inviting belief
contextNote.text: Paul is the one on trial, yet verse 27 questions the king. Agrippa answers that Paul is trying to make him a Christian (verse 28). Verse 29 takes that answer and widens it. Paul wishes it for Agrippa and for all who hear him. He wants them to be as he is, with one thing left out. “Except for these bonds” points to the chains he wears. Verse 31 gives the hearers’ verdict: nothing he did deserves death or bonds.

passages.title: Promised survival still requires food, sailors, and restraint
passages.summary: Paul sails for Italy under a centurion named Julius. At Fair Havens he warns that the voyage will bring loss. The centurion follows the pilot and the owner, and they sail on. A violent wind drives the ship for many days. Paul says an angel told him no life will be lost. On the fourteenth night the sailors try to leave in the boat. Paul urges all 276 people to eat. The ship breaks up on a shore, and everyone reaches land.

lds.text: The selected lesson applies the voyage to following the Lord’s servants. Why do promised lives still require the sailors to remain aboard?

contextNote.title: Promised survival still requires food, sailors, and restraint
contextNote.text: Verse 24 promises that all who sail with Paul will live. Verse 30 then shows sailors lowering the boat to escape. Verse 31 says the soldiers cannot be saved unless the sailors stay. The promise does not remove the need for the crew. The soldiers believe Paul this time and cut the ropes (verse 32). In verse 11 the centurion had trusted the pilot over him. Verse 44 reports the result: all escape safely to land.

passages.title: The ending leaves Paul bound while teaching continues
passages.summary: The survivors land on Malta, and the islanders show them kindness. A viper bites Paul, and he shakes it off unharmed. He heals the father of Publius and others. After three months they sail to Italy, and believers meet Paul on the road. In Rome Paul lives under guard and calls the Jewish leaders. He explains his case and teaches them from morning to evening. Some believe, and some do not. Paul quotes Isaiah, and for two years he receives all who come.

lds.text: Why does the book end with teaching rather than the appeal’s final verdict?

contextNote.title: The ending leaves Paul bound while teaching continues
contextNote.text: The book has moved toward Rome since 23:11. It does not report the hearing before Caesar. Verse 30 says Paul stayed two years in a rented house. Verse 16 says a soldier guarded him. Verse 31 says what he did there: he taught about God’s kingdom and Jesus. The last words are “without hindrance.” Paul is held, but the teaching is not.

events.title: Waiting prepares witnesses for a task larger than their question
events.summary: The writer opens a second book for Theophilus. The risen Jesus teaches the apostles for forty days. He tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit. They ask if he will now restore the kingdom to Israel. He is taken up, and two men in white speak to them. About 120 believers pray together in an upper room. Peter says another witness must take the place of Judas. They pray and cast lots, and the lot falls on Matthias.
events.detail: The apostles ask about timing in verse 6. Will the kingdom come back to Israel now? Verse 7 says the times are not theirs to know. Verse 8 gives them a task in place of a date. Power will come with the Holy Spirit, not from their own plan. The task moves outward: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. Verse 22 defines a witness: one who saw Jesus from John’s baptism onward.

events.title: Many languages lead toward shared life
events.summary: On the day of Pentecost a sound like wind fills the house. Tongues like fire rest on the believers, and they speak in other languages. Jews from many nations hear their own languages. Some are amazed, and others say the speakers are drunk. Peter quotes Joel and says God raised Jesus from the dead. The hearers ask what they should do. Peter tells them to repent and be baptized. About three thousand join, and they share teaching, meals, prayer, and goods.
events.detail: The hearers are cut to the heart and ask what to do (verse 37). Verse 38 answers with repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Verse 39 says how far that gift reaches. It is for the hearers, their children, and all who are far off. Joel’s words in verse 17 already said “all flesh.” The list of nations in verses 9–11 shows who is listening. The limit in verse 39 is God’s call, not place or birth.

events.title: A healing redirects attention away from the healers
events.summary: Peter and John go to the temple at the hour of prayer. A man lame from birth asks them for money at the gate. Peter says he has no silver or gold. He tells the man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ. The man leaps, walks, and praises God in the temple. A crowd runs together in Solomon’s porch. Peter says God raised Jesus, whom they had denied. He says they acted in ignorance and calls them to repent.
events.detail: The crowd runs to Peter and John in wonder (verse 11). Verse 12 asks why, and it names their wrong guess. They think the two men’s own power or godliness made him walk. Verse 13 gives the credit to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 16 says faith in Jesus’ name made the man strong. Peter speaks to this crowd about its own acts (verses 13–15). Verse 17 then says they acted in ignorance, and verse 19 offers repentance.

events.title: A visible witness limits the council's threat
events.summary: The priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees arrest Peter and John. The next day the rulers ask by what name they acted. Peter says the man stands healed by the name of Jesus. The council sees their boldness and notes they are untrained men. It orders them not to speak in Jesus’ name. Peter and John say they cannot stop telling what they saw. The believers pray for boldness, and the place shakes. They share goods, and Barnabas sells a field for those in need.
events.detail: The council has a problem in verses 14–16. The healed man stands there, and all Jerusalem knows the sign. They cannot deny it, so they try to stop the speech (verse 17). Verse 19 asks them to judge: listen to them or to God. Verse 20 gives the reason the order cannot work. The two men saw and heard these things themselves. Verse 21 shows the result: the council threatens and lets them go.

events.title: Deceit threatens trust within a sharing community
events.summary: Ananias and Sapphira sell land and keep part of the price. They bring the rest as if it were the whole. Peter says Ananias lied to God, and Ananias falls dead. Three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and also dies. The apostles heal many in Solomon’s porch. The high priest and the Sadducees jail them, but an angel opens the doors. Before the council Peter says they must obey God rather than men. Gamaliel advises caution, and the apostles are beaten and released.
events.detail: Chapter 4 ended with Barnabas giving the full price of a field. Ananias brings a part and lets it stand as the whole (verses 1–2). Verse 4 makes clear what the wrong is. The land was his, and the money was his to use. No rule made him give it all. The wrong is the lie, and verse 4 says it was told to God. Verse 11 reports the result: great fear on the whole assembly.

events.title: Unequal care produces a shared decision
events.summary: The number of disciples grows. The Hellenists, Jewish believers who spoke Greek, complain against the Hebrews. Their widows are being missed in the daily serving. The twelve ask the group to choose seven men for this work. The group chooses Stephen, Philip, and five others, and the apostles lay hands on them. The word spreads, and many priests believe. Stephen works signs, and men from a synagogue argue with him. They bring false witnesses and take him before the council.
events.detail: The complaint in verse 1 is about daily help for widows. The twelve say they should not leave the word to serve tables (verse 2). Verse 3 gives the choice to the whole group. It also sets the test: good report, the Spirit, and wisdom. The apostles keep prayer and the word as their own work (verse 4). Verse 5 says the plan pleased the whole group, and it names the seven. Verse 7 reports the result: the word of God increased.

events.title: Stephen's answer follows rejected helpers and God's wider presence
events.summary: The high priest asks Stephen if the charges are true. Stephen answers with Israel’s history. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia and was with Joseph in Egypt. Moses was pushed away by his own people, yet God sent him. The fathers made a calf in the wilderness. They had the tabernacle, and Solomon built a house. Stephen says his hearers resist the Holy Spirit as their fathers did. They stone him, and he prays that the sin not be held against them.
events.detail: Stephen is charged with speaking against the holy place (6:13–14). His answer shows God at work far from it. God acts in Mesopotamia (verse 2), Egypt (verse 9), and Sinai (verse 30). Verse 33 calls desert ground holy. Verse 48 then says the Most High does not live in houses made by hands. Verses 49–50 quote Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne, and his hand made all things. The charge is about a place, and the answer is about where God is.

events.title: Scattering brings witness and a question about Scripture
events.summary: Saul approves of Stephen’s death, and a great persecution scatters the believers. Philip tells the people of Samaria about Christ, and many are baptized. Simon, who had amazed the city with sorcery, is baptized too. Peter and John come and lay hands on them, and they receive the Holy Spirit. Simon offers money for that power, and Peter rebukes him. An angel sends Philip to a desert road. An Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah in his chariot. Philip tells him about Jesus and baptizes him.
events.detail: The official has the scroll and reads it aloud (verses 28 and 30). Philip asks if he understands. Verse 31 says he cannot without a guide, and he invites Philip up. His question in verse 34 is exact: does the prophet mean himself or another? Philip starts from that passage and tells him about Jesus (verse 35). Simon wanted to buy a power (verses 18–19). The official asks for an explanation, and then for baptism (verse 36).

events.title: Saul's changed direction requires other people's trust
events.summary: Saul travels to Damascus with letters to arrest followers of the Way. A light from the sky stops him, and a voice says it is Jesus. He is blind for three days. The Lord sends a disciple named Ananias to him. Ananias lays hands on Saul, and Saul sees and is baptized. Saul speaks of Jesus in the synagogues, and opponents plot to kill him. Barnabas brings him to the apostles in Jerusalem. Peter heals Aeneas in Lydda and raises Tabitha in Joppa.
events.detail: The Lord tells Ananias to go to Saul (verse 11). Verse 13 is his objection: many have reported Saul’s evil in Jerusalem. Verse 14 adds that Saul holds authority to bind believers in Damascus too. The Lord does not deny the reports. He calls Saul a chosen vessel (verse 15). Ananias goes and calls him “Brother Saul” (verse 17). In verses 26–27 the disciples fear Saul until Barnabas speaks for him.

events.title: The Spirit's arrival changes Peter's judgment
events.summary: Cornelius is a centurion in Caesarea who fears God and gives to the poor. An angel tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. Peter sees a sheet full of animals and hears a voice tell him to eat. He refuses, and the voice says not to call unclean what God cleansed. The Spirit tells him to go with the messengers. In Cornelius’s house Peter says God shows no favoritism. The Holy Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers while he speaks. Peter orders that they be baptized.
events.detail: Peter says in verse 28 that a Jew may not visit another nation. God has shown him to call no person unclean. Verse 34 states the lesson: God does not show favoritism. Verses 44–46 then give proof that the Jewish believers can hear. The Gentiles speak in other languages and praise God. Verse 47 asks a question that expects no objection. They have the Spirit “just like us,” so water cannot be refused.

events.title: Peter must explain the meal and the shared gift
events.summary: Believers in Jerusalem criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. Peter tells them the vision, the Spirit’s order, and the angel’s message to Cornelius. He says the Spirit fell on that household as on them at the beginning. They fall silent and then glorify God. Scattered believers reach Antioch, and some speak to Greeks. Barnabas comes, and he brings Saul from Tarsus. The disciples are first called Christians in Antioch. They send famine relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul.
events.detail: The charge in verse 3 is about a meal, not about baptism. Peter answers in order (verse 4), and he lists what God did. The vision came three times (verse 10). The Spirit told him to go (verse 12). The Spirit fell as he began to speak (verse 15). Verse 17 ends with a question: who was he to stand against God? Verse 18 shows the hearers accept it: God gave repentance to the Gentiles too.

events.title: An opened prison meets a closed household gate
events.summary: King Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword. He arrests Peter during the days of unleavened bread. The assembly prays for Peter. At night an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, and the iron gate opens. Peter goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark. A servant named Rhoda hears his voice and runs in without opening the gate. Herod orders the guards put to death. Later he accepts praise as a god, and an angel strikes him.
events.detail: Verse 5 says the assembly prayed constantly for Peter. Verse 12 shows many still praying when he knocks. Yet verse 15 has them call Rhoda crazy. Then they say it must be his angel. They prayed for him and did not expect him at the gate. Peter himself thought the rescue was a vision (verse 9). Verse 16 ends it plainly: they open the gate, see him, and are amazed.

events.title: A synagogue invitation becomes a dispute over wider hearing
events.summary: The Holy Spirit tells the assembly at Antioch to set apart Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the sorcerer Elymas opposes them and is struck blind. The proconsul Sergius Paulus believes. In Antioch of Pisidia the synagogue rulers invite Paul to speak. He tells Israel’s history from Egypt to David and says God raised Jesus. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers. Some Jewish hearers contradict Paul, and he turns to the Gentiles. The two are driven out and go on to Iconium.
events.detail: The first Sabbath ends well: many Jews and converts follow Paul (verse 43). The turn comes in verses 44–45, when the whole city gathers. Verse 45 says jealousy at the crowds moved those who contradicted him. Verse 46 answers that group in that city. The word had to come to them first, and they pushed it away. Verse 47 quotes Isaiah on a light for the Gentiles. Paul still starts in the synagogue in the next city (14:1).

events.title: Praise and violence both misunderstand the visiting teachers
events.summary: In Iconium Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue, and the city divides. They flee a plan to stone them. In Lystra Paul heals a man who had never walked. The crowd calls them Jupiter and Mercury, and a priest brings oxen to sacrifice. The two tear their clothes and say they are only men. Opponents from Antioch and Iconium arrive, and the crowd stones Paul. He gets up and goes on to Derbe. They return through the cities, appoint elders, and report in Antioch.
events.detail: The crowd explains the healing in its own terms: gods have come down (verse 11). Verse 15 refuses the honor in two steps. The two are men “of the same nature” as the crowd. Their news is to turn from these things to the living God. Paul quotes no Scripture in this speech. He points to the maker of sky, earth, and sea. Verse 17 names the witness this crowd already has: rain, harvests, and food.

events.title: A disputed requirement leads to a letter and trusted messengers
events.summary: Men from Judea teach in Antioch that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute this and go to Jerusalem. The apostles and elders meet. Peter says God gave the Gentiles the Spirit and made no distinction. James quotes the prophets and proposes four things to avoid. They send a letter with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices. Paul and Barnabas then disagree over John Mark and part ways. Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia.
events.detail: The question in verses 1 and 5 is whether Gentiles must keep Moses’ law. Peter calls that a yoke their fathers could not bear (verse 10). Verse 28 gives the answer in the letter’s own words. It names two who agree: the Holy Spirit and “us.” The word “burden” answers Peter’s “yoke.” Only four things remain, listed in verse 29. Verse 31 shows how the readers took it: they rejoiced at the encouragement.

events.title: Lost income becomes a public charge and a prison crisis
events.summary: Paul takes Timothy with him from Lystra. A vision of a man from Macedonia calls Paul across the sea. In Philippi Lydia, a seller of purple, believes and hosts them. Paul orders a spirit out of a slave girl who told fortunes. Her owners lose their income and accuse Paul and Silas before the magistrates. The two are beaten and jailed, and an earthquake opens the doors at midnight. The jailer and his household are baptized. Paul says they are Romans, and the magistrates come and ask them to leave.
events.detail: The jailer was ordered to keep them safely (verse 23). Verse 27 shows what open doors mean to him. He thinks the prisoners are gone, and he draws his sword on himself. Verse 28 stops him with a fact: all are still there. The men he chained now save his life. His question in verse 30 follows: what must he do to be saved? Verses 33–34 show the change: he washes their wounds and feeds them.

events.title: Paul changes his starting point for different hearers
events.summary: In Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths. Some believe, and opponents raise a mob against Jason’s house. In Beroea the hearers examine the Scriptures daily. In Athens Paul is troubled by the city’s idols. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus. He speaks of the God who made the world and needs nothing. He quotes their poets and says God will judge through a man he raised. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe.
events.detail: In the synagogue Paul argues from the Scriptures (verses 2–3). At the Areopagus he quotes no Scripture. Verse 23 starts with an altar of the Athenians’ own. Its words admit there is a god they do not know. Paul says he will announce that one. He then quotes their poets, not the prophets (verse 28). Verse 31 ends with the same claim: God raised a man from the dead.

events.title: Teaching develops through work, hospitality, and correction
events.summary: In Corinth Paul lives and works with Aquila and Priscilla, who are tentmakers. He reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposed, he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid. The proconsul Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish law. Paul sails to Ephesus, Caesarea, and Antioch. In Ephesus Apollos teaches well but knows only John’s baptism.
events.detail: Verses 24–25 praise Apollos first. He is eloquent, strong in the Scriptures, and accurate about Jesus. One thing is missing: he knows only the baptism of John. Verse 26 shows how the gap is closed. Priscilla and Aquila hear him and take him aside. They explain the way of God “more accurately.” Verses 27–28 show the result: he greatly helps the believers in Achaia.

events.title: Changed worship threatens a trade and gathers a confused crowd
events.summary: In Ephesus Paul meets twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism. He baptizes them in Jesus’ name, and they receive the Holy Spirit. He teaches for two years in the school of Tyrannus. Seven sons of Sceva misuse Jesus’ name, and a possessed man beats them. Many burn their books of magic. Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, gathers the craftsmen. A crowd fills the theater and shouts for two hours. The town clerk sends them home and points to the courts.
events.detail: Verse 25 opens Demetrius’s speech with money. The craftsmen have their wealth from this business. Verse 26 names the threat: Paul says gods made by hands are no gods. Only in verse 27 does he add the honor of Artemis and her temple. The crowd takes up the second reason and shouts her name (verse 28). Verse 32 says most did not know why they had come. The clerk points them to the courts (verses 35–38).

events.title: Paul's farewell makes care more important than personal gain
events.summary: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece and returns by way of Troas. There Paul speaks until midnight, and young Eutychus falls from a window. Paul embraces him, and he is brought in alive. At Miletus Paul calls the elders of Ephesus. He says he taught them openly and house to house. Verse 34 says his own hands paid for him and his companions. Verse 35 turns that record into a pattern for the elders. They are to work so that they can help the weak. The saying of Jesus gives the reason: giving is more blessed than receiving.

events.title: Warnings and an untested accusation lead toward arrest
events.summary: Paul sails to Tyre and then to Caesarea, where he stays with Philip. The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt. He says Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul says he is ready to die there. James and the elders report a rumor that he teaches Jews to leave Moses. They ask him to join four men in a vow at the temple. Men from Asia see him there and stir up the crowd. Roman soldiers take him, and he asks to speak.
events.detail: Verse 28 makes two charges: Paul teaches against the temple and brought Greeks in. Verse 29 gives the basis for the second charge. The accusers saw Trophimus with Paul in the city. They “supposed” the rest. Paul was in fact there to complete a purification (verse 26). Verse 34 shows the crowd’s state: the officer could not learn the facts.

events.title: Paul's defense reaches its breaking point with the Gentile task
events.summary: Paul speaks to the crowd in Hebrew, and they grow quiet. He says he is a Jew, taught by Gamaliel, and once persecuted the Way. He tells of the light near Damascus and the voice of Jesus. Ananias, a devout man, told him he would be a witness. Later, praying in the temple, he was told to leave Jerusalem. When he says he was sent to the Gentiles, the crowd shouts for his death. The officer orders him flogged. Paul says he is a Roman citizen by birth, and they stop.
events.detail: The crowd listens through the whole account of Jesus’ voice and Ananias. Verse 22 says they listened “until he said that.” The breaking point is verse 21, not the vision. Paul says the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles. He says this came while he prayed in the temple (verse 17). He even objected that Jerusalem knew his past (verses 19–20). The crowd in 21:28 already charged him with bringing Greeks in.

events.title: A promise of Rome passes through a divided hearing and a hidden plot
events.summary: Paul tells the council he has lived in good conscience. The high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul says he is a Pharisee, on trial for the hope of resurrection. Pharisees and Sadducees then argue, and the officer pulls him out. That night the Lord tells him he must testify in Rome. More than forty men vow not to eat until they kill him. Paul’s nephew reports the plot to the officer. Soldiers take Paul by night to the governor Felix in Caesarea.
events.detail: Verse 10 leaves Paul in the barracks after a hearing that settled nothing. The officer feared he would be torn apart. Verse 11 comes that night and gives the one fixed point. As he testified in Jerusalem, he must testify in Rome. A sworn plot tests that word at once (verses 12–13). The way out is ordinary: a nephew hears and reports (verse 16). Verse 23 sends Paul out alive under 470 guards.

events.title: A delayed hearing preserves the governor's advantage
events.summary: The high priest Ananias and a speaker named Tertullus bring charges before Felix. Tertullus calls Paul a plague and a leader of the Nazarene sect. He says Paul tried to profane the temple. Paul answers that no one found him arguing or stirring a crowd. He says he worships the God of his fathers and hopes for a resurrection. Felix puts off the case until Lysias comes. He and his wife Drusilla hear Paul, and Felix becomes afraid. He keeps Paul two years and leaves him bound.
events.detail: Felix knows the Way well and still delays the ruling (verse 22). Verse 25 shows one reason. Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and judgment, and Felix is terrified. Verse 26 gives a second reason, and it is money. He hopes Paul will pay for release, so he sends for him often. Verse 27 adds a third: he wants favor with Paul’s accusers. After two years Paul is still bound, with no ruling given.

events.title: Paul's appeal creates a journey without a clear written charge
events.summary: Festus replaces Felix, and the chief priests ask him to send Paul to Jerusalem. They plan an ambush on the road. Festus hears the case in Caesarea, and the charges are not proved. He asks if Paul will be tried in Jerusalem. Paul says he stands at Caesar’s court and appeals to Caesar. Festus agrees to send him. King Agrippa and Bernice visit, and Festus explains the case. He brings Paul before them the next day.
events.detail: Paul’s appeal in verse 11 binds Festus to send him (verse 12). That leaves the governor with a letter he cannot write. Verse 25 says he found nothing deserving death. Verse 26 says he has nothing certain to write to the emperor. Verse 19 shows why: the dispute is about Jesus, whom Paul says is alive. Verse 27 states the difficulty in Festus’s own words. A prisoner sent with no charge makes no sense, so he asks Agrippa’s help.

events.title: Paul answers a royal hearing by inviting belief
events.summary: Paul speaks before King Agrippa, Bernice, and Festus. He says he lived as a Pharisee and now stands trial for Israel’s hope. He tells how he jailed the saints and voted for their deaths. He describes the light on the Damascus road and the voice of Jesus. He says he obeyed the vision and taught Jews and Gentiles to repent. Festus shouts that learning has made him mad. Paul asks Agrippa if he believes the prophets. Agrippa says Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed.

Paul wishes it for Agrippa and for all who hear him. He wants them to be as he is, with one thing left out. “Except for these bonds” points to the chains he wears. Verse 31 gives the hearers’ verdict: nothing he did deserves death or bonds.

events.title: Promised survival still requires food, sailors, and restraint
events.summary: Paul sails for Italy under a centurion named Julius. At Fair Havens he warns that the voyage will bring loss. The centurion follows the pilot and the owner, and they sail on. A violent wind drives the ship for many days. Paul says an angel told him no life will be lost. On the fourteenth night the sailors try to leave in the boat. Paul urges all 276 people to eat. The ship breaks up on a shore, and everyone reaches land.
events.detail: Verse 24 promises that all who sail with Paul will live. Verse 30 then shows sailors lowering the boat to escape. Verse 31 says the soldiers cannot be saved unless the sailors stay. The promise does not remove the need for the crew. The soldiers believe Paul this time and cut the ropes (verse 32). In verse 11 the centurion had trusted the pilot over him. Verse 44 reports the result: all escape safely to land.

events.title: The ending leaves Paul bound while teaching continues
events.summary: The survivors land on Malta, and the islanders show them kindness. A viper bites Paul, and he shakes it off unharmed. He heals the father of Publius and others. After three months they sail to Italy, and believers meet Paul on the road. In Rome Paul lives under guard and calls the Jewish leaders. He explains his case and teaches them from morning to evening. Some believe, and some do not. Paul quotes Isaiah, and for two years he receives all who come.
events.detail: The book has moved toward Rome since 23:11. It does not report the hearing before Caesar. Verse 30 says Paul stayed two years in a rented house. Verse 16 says a soldier guarded him. Verse 31 says what he did there: he taught about God’s kingdom and Jesus. The last words are “without hindrance.” Paul is held, but the teaching is not.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: Acts: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Unequal care produces a shared decision
steps.text: The complaint in verse 1 is about daily help for widows. The twelve say they should not leave the word to serve tables (verse 2). Verse 3 gives the choice to the whole group. It also sets the test: good report, the Spirit, and wisdom. The apostles keep prayer and the word as their own work (verse 4). Verse 5 says the plan pleased the whole group, and it names the seven. Verse 7 reports the result: the word of God increased.

steps.title: The Spirit's arrival changes Peter's judgment
steps.text: Peter says in verse 28 that a Jew may not visit another nation. God has shown him to call no person unclean. Verse 34 states the lesson: God does not show favoritism. Verses 44–46 then give proof that the Jewish believers can hear. The Gentiles speak in other languages and praise God. Verse 47 asks a question that expects no objection. They have the Spirit “just like us,” so water cannot be refused.

steps.title: A disputed requirement leads to a letter and trusted messengers
steps.text: The question in verses 1 and 5 is whether Gentiles must keep Moses’ law. Peter calls that a yoke their fathers could not bear (verse 10). Verse 28 gives the answer in the letter’s own words. It names two who agree: the Holy Spirit and “us.” The word “burden” answers Peter’s “yoke.” Only four things remain, listed in verse 29. Verse 31 shows how the readers took it: they rejoiced at the encouragement.

steps.title: Promised survival still requires food, sailors, and restraint
steps.text: Verse 24 promises that all who sail with Paul will live. Verse 30 then shows sailors lowering the boat to escape. Verse 31 says the soldiers cannot be saved unless the sailors stay. The promise does not remove the need for the crew. The soldiers believe Paul this time and cut the ropes (verse 32). In verse 11 the centurion had trusted the pilot over him. Verse 44 reports the result: all escape safely to land.
